note:
The National Army Museum gives a garrison of 150, including hospital patients, against 4,000 Zulu warriors, with 17 British and about 400 Zulu dead. Wounds are described qualitatively and are not converted into a casualty count. The representative British rifle and Zulu spear do not imply that all defenders were fit to fight or that every Zulu warrior carried the same weapon.

The reviewed British infantry component uses a foreign-service helmet and single-shot Martini-Henry breech-loading rifle with socket bayonet. The National Army Museum identifies the weapon type at Rorke’s Drift, preserves a dated Mk II rifle, and holds Lady Butler’s 1879 study of survivor David Jenkins showing the helmet and fixed bayonet. Extension to the British infantry component at Isandlwana and Ulundi is a disclosed same-campaign analogy. This replaces the earlier forage-cap musket family for the British component only; African auxiliaries, cavalry, artillery, exact regimental dress and their proportions are not reconstructed. All existing participant identities, strengths, casualty categories and Zulu equipment assignments remain unchanged.
